item.title: Axis Bank Q2FY27 result: Profit rises 38% to ₹7,003 crore, misses estimates
item.description: Net interest income rose 11.8 per cent to ₹15,371 crore, while loans grew 23 per cent and provisions fell 52.2 per cent; other income declined 1.4 per cent to ₹6,531 crore ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Indian private-sector lender Axis Bank reported on Saturday a quarterly profit that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as higher operating expenses and weaker other income offset robust credit growth and lower provisions.Axis Bank, the country's third-largest private bank by assets, posted a stand-alone net profit of ₹7,003 crore ($737.5 million) for the quarter ended on September 30, compared with ₹5,090 crore a year earlier.Analysts, on average, had forecast a profit of ₹7,124 crore, according to LSEG-compiled data.Other income, which includes earnings from bonds and other investments, fell 1.4 per cent to ₹6,531 crore.Rising bond yields and volatility in the rupee during the quarter weighed on treasury income at the Mumbai-based lender, tempering earnings even as lending expanded across segments.Banks across India reported strong loan growth during the quarter across corporate and retail portfolios.Net interest income grew 11.8 per cent to ₹15,371 crore, helped by a 23 per cent rise in total loans. Deposits increased 20.7 per cent from a year earlier.Provisions for potential bad loans and other contingencies fell 52.2 per cent to ₹1,694 crore.The gross non-performing asset ratio stood at 1.16 per cent at end-September, compared with 1.28 per cent three months earlier.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Pope Leo returns to Vatican after lung cancer surgery, recovery on track

Pope Leo returns to Vatican after lung cancer surgery, recovery on track Leo, 71, had greeted patients inside the hospital before waving to well-wishers outside as he walked to the waiting vehicle

Pope Leo waves as he leaves Gemelli Hospital following his lung surgery and cancer diagnosis, in Rome, Italy (Photo: Reuters)

AP Vatican City 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 17 2026 | 8:28 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Pope Leo returned to the Vatican on Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where dozens of well-wishers saw him off with cries of "Holiness."   "I am better, thank you," the pope said when asked how he was as he was driven away in a black SUV. Leo, 71, had greeted patients inside the hospital before waving to well-wishers outside as he walked to the waiting vehicle. He briefly stopped when a teenage girl presented him with a homemade papal doll. His surgeon, Dr Stefano Margaritora, head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli, accompanied him to the hospital door as he was formally discharged.

Ten minutes after leaving the hospital, the pope entered the Vatican gates. He is due to greet the faithful with the traditional Angelus blessing on Sunday, a week after announcing that doctors had found a nodule on his lung. In an unusually candid disclosure, he said it would be removed. Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Also Read

Pope diagnosed with lung cancer, part of right lung removed, says Vatican

Antibiotic resistance emerging as major threat to surgical care: Experts

Pope Leo seeks strict AI rules, warns against profit-driven race

Marco Rubio urges Europe to act on Iran during Italy, Vatican visit

Marco Rubio discusses West Asia with Pope after Trump dispute

Since the surgery, Leo has shown signs of recovering well. He had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, held meetings with senior aides and celebrated Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.

Medical bulletins from his personal physician and surgeon also described a good postoperative recovery, saying he had been able to carry on "normal daily activities completely on his own."   On Friday, the Vatican released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him in green vestments standing at an altar in the hospital chapel. Doctors said tests confirmed his "continued improvement."   Leo presided alone over the liturgy and distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes, Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said. In his homily, he thanked hospital staff "for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him," Bruni said.

The Vatican had initially estimated a weeklong hospital stay and cancelled his audiences through Tuesday. Experts said patients could be discharged earlier depending on their recovery, while Bruni said the decision rested with the pope's doctors. Leo's next major engagement is a trip to Latin America from Nov. 6-17, giving him about three more weeks to recover before an ambitious journey that includes a dozen flights and two helicopter trips. The Vatican signalled that preparations were proceeding by publishing on Friday the names of journalists accredited to travel on Leo's plane. Oncology surgeons say patients are generally cleared to fly after three weeks, provided their recovery allows.

Doctors are still awaiting test results to determine the cancer's precise molecular and genetic makeup, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether further treatment is necessary.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Sisi says Egypt will not amend Constitution, rules out staying past 2030

Sisi says Egypt will not amend Constitution, rules out staying past 2030 Sisi, 71, is serving a six-year term after being reelected in December 2023

Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi (File Photo)

Reuters 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 17 2026 | 7:49 PM IST

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months before then.   The proposal gives the Egyptian Military Academy a central role in preparing future leaders, underscoring the armed forces' influence beyond national defence. Under Sisi, a former general, the military has expanded its presence in the economy and civilian affairs.   Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the academy, Sisi said a committee overseen by the speaker of parliament and including intellectuals, politicians and the ministers of higher education and justice, would develop criteria for selecting candidates and draft legislation for the training programme.

Reiterating that Egypt's constitution would not be amended, he said the end of his presidential term in 2030 was "a matter that has been completely settled and will not be discussed".   He said the programme would allow Egyptians to "elect and choose from among" its graduates, but gave no details on how they would be put forward for elected or appointed posts. Also Read

The Mecca agreement is fuelled by regional concerns, say experts premium

Nine large banks engaged in so-called debanking, says US regulator

Jeffrey Archer, novelist whose real life rivaled his thrillers, dies at 86

Broadcom to lend Anthropic up to $42 bn to lease its chips, filing says

Iran bombing could ramp up after midterm elections: Donald Trump

"I will not leave the Egyptian state except when it is replete with sons and daughters capable of assuming responsibility," Sisi said.   The programme would target PhD holders from reputable Egyptian and foreign universities, who would spend 30 months ??at the academy learning about the state, its resources and how to preserve them, Sisi said. He said graduates would be prepared for leadership roles ranging from the presidency to ministries, governorates and parliament.

Sisi, 71, is serving a six-year term after being reelected in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four to six years and allowed him to seek a third term, clearing the way for him to remain in office until 2030.   The latest in a line of Egyptian rulers drawn from the military, he became president in 2014, a year after toppling Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood - Egypt's first democratically elected leader - following mass protests.   He proceeded to crush the Brotherhood, the Middle East's oldest Islamist organisation, and maintain a grip on power.

item.title: Apple appoints Meta veteran Scott Tucker to lead global litigation
item.description: Tucker will oversee commercial and patent litigation worldwide and legal matters involving Apple's financial services as the company faces mounting lawsuits under General Counsel Jennifer Newstead ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Mark Gurman Apple Inc. has tapped a longtime Meta Platforms Inc. executive as its new litigation chief, bolstering its legal team at a time when the iPhone maker faces a growing array of lawsuits. The company has hired Scott Tucker, a longtime deputy general counsel and litigation chief at Meta, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The move reunites Tucker with new Apple General Counsel Jennifer Newstead, who is bringing on a trusted lieutenant from her time at the social networking giant. Tucker is becoming Apple’s vice president of global litigation and financial services, a newly created position overseeing commercial and patent litigation worldwide, said the people, who asked not to be named because the move isn’t public. He’ll also manage legal matters involving the company’s financial offerings.  The appointment means Heather Grenier, Apple’s current vice president of commercial and competition litigation, will move one level lower in the organisation, reporting to Tucker instead of directly to Newstead. Grenier will still remain on Newstead’s legal leadership team.  Tucker, in addition to his tenure at Meta, previously held a senior legal position at Morgan Stanley, giving him experience relevant to his new financial services responsibilities. Newstead took over as Apple’s general counsel in March after serving as Meta’s top lawyer for six years. Kyle Andeer, another senior member of Apple’s legal department and its longtime vice president managing regulatory and product-related legal matters, is seeing his role expand. He is gaining oversight of international legal matters and functions involving online child safety, cybersecurity and law enforcement. Spokespeople for Apple and Meta declined to comment.  The changes are part of a broader reorganisation under Newstead, who oversees legal and government affairs. Apple recently hired Nate Gatten, a former American Airlines Group Inc. executive, as its vice president of government affairs. The company has also appointed new government affairs leads for different international regions. Apple combined its legal and government affairs groups under Newstead following the recent retirements of Lisa Jackson, the former head of environmental, policy and social initiatives, and previous top lawyer Kate Adams. Former Chief Executive Officer Tim Cook, now the company’s executive chairman, has also taken a leading role in government affairs. Apple is waging a variety of legal battles, including a sweeping US antitrust lawsuit, its long-running dispute with Epic Games Inc. over App Store restrictions, and litigation related to privacy and delays to Siri features. The company has faced billions of dollars in judgments and settlements in recent years, while regulators in the US and Europe have challenged business practices central to the iPhone maker’s operations. Some Apple executives believe the company hasn’t fared as well in court as it should have, particularly in litigation involving the App Store. Those setbacks have forced Apple to change its commission structure and the circumstances under which it can charge developers. The changes threaten to significantly slow growth in Apple’s services business, a key driver of revenue expansion in recent years. A slowdown in that business would deal a major blow to the company’s overall financial performance. Even in the best of times, overseeing Apple’s litigation is a difficult job. The Cupertino, California-based company is among the most frequently sued businesses in the world, facing cases ranging from slip-and-fall claims at its retail stores to multibillion-dollar antitrust disputes. Grenier took over the role under particularly challenging circumstances, replacing her predecessor just before Apple’s landmark trial against Epic Games began in 2021. Her tenure has also spanned two major leadership transitions: the appointment of John Ternus as CEO and Newstead’s arrival. In recent weeks, Ternus has overseen a sweeping series of executive changes, including the appointment of new leaders for the App Store, events and corporate functions such as information security and real estate. The reshuffling also includes the departure of the longtime Apple Pay chief, the replacement of the company’s mergers and acquisitions head, and a reorganisation of the company’s hardware engineering division.
